question: Is a woman's marriage valid if her husband belongs to a different sect of Islam?
asked: A sister in our community got married to a man from a different sect of Islam, and she didn't have much knowledge about that sect. Now that they have two kids and these religious differences are coming to the forefront, she is wondering whether her marriage is valid or not, and whether she should continue or not.
answer:
This is a very personal question, but it is dealing with someone in our own community, so because of this, I'm answering it. Otherwise, I would not have taken this question. And also I will change some of the details, because it is not my habit to mention specific groups.

I'm not going to answer specifically for this sister. Even if in our community, she needs to come to me or somebody and speak to me directly, so I can get more details, and also speak to the husband. But I will speak generically. I'm not going to mention the group's name, but I'll mention one or two details so that the sister knows that it is her case that I'm talking about. This is a group that was formed in India around a thousand years ago... no, sorry, not a thousand years ago; six hundred years ago. Six hundred years ago, there was a person in India who claimed to be the Mahdi, and he was from a village called Jaunpur. And this is a sect, a small, minuscule sect; not a lot of people are aware of this group. And her husband is from this group. And when she got married, she didn't know anything much about this group, and now it's coming to the forefront.

So the general rule, and I'm going to be very careful here, the general rule that I have, and this is an ethical and a moral advice, not a fiqhi one: **we should marry people who have similar religious backgrounds as we do.** Why? This sister is explaining exactly why, what's going to happen. Generally speaking, most Muslims are so-so religious, not that religious. Okay, that's the way people are. I'm not endorsing it; it's the way it is. But then usually, and it is Allah's Sunnah and qadr, usually five, ten years down the line, one of the two gets more religious, right? And this is when the issues come. When they first got married, they didn't care that much about religion, or they agreed to respect each other's personal religious rituals. Good enough, okay. But then there's going to be a clash of schedules. Then there's going to be debates over dinner. And then the kids: who's going to raise the kids in which religious strand? And then which mosque are they going to go to? And then which interpretation are they going to be taught?

So all of these things, most couples, when they're newly married or before marriage, when they're falling in love and whatnot, they don't think these things through. And that's why elders have a huge point of wisdom here that our youngsters don't understand: that birds of a feather flock together. People of a similar background, similar mindset, similar, you know, even socio-economic. Even though, of course, it's allowed to do whatever you want, as long as it's halal in Islam. It's allowed to marry completely different; no problem at all. But generally speaking, human society has shown that when there is compatibility... And compatibility is born not just because of the excitement of an interesting dinner-table conversation. No, compatibility is long-term: 30, 40 years of a life lived together. This generally means you have shared values, shared backgrounds, shared upbringings, shared religious values.

Now again, technically, it is halal to marry any Muslim from any group of Islam that is within the mainstream of Islam. And this group that the sister mentions, I will not mention its name, this group is within Islam. It has beliefs that are different than ours. It believes that the Mahdi has come and gone, and they believe in the Mahdi, but they don't believe in another prophet. If there is a group that believes in another prophet, that Allah sends wahy down, and they call their founder a nabi or a rasul, or whatever technical term they want to use, and they believe he is sent by Allah as a prophet, then this is a red line that expels this group from the fold of Islam. Just like if somebody believed in a God besides Allah, and they said, "We believe in another creator," it doesn't matter if they call themselves Muslim; they are not Muslim.

So the group that the sister is asking about does not have deviations to that level. It believes in a Mahdi figure. And we as Sunnis believe in a Mahdi. The Shia believe that the Mahdi is existent. This group believes the Mahdi has come and died. This is yet another group out there, and they do have certain differences from our groups. But as somebody who knows theology, and my expertise is aqidah and theology, I am aware of this group, and I have studied their writings from their sources, and I have studied this group to the extent that I'm interested in studying, and I have not seen anything that would consider this group to be outside the fold of Islam. Rather, they are a group that has their differences from us, and I would not encourage intermarriage.

But now that this is the case, and you already have two children, generally speaking, if the marriage is sustainable and it is going along fine, then for the sake of the children you should think about staying and whatnot. It's not something that is a matter of iman and kufr. However, if you were to find out that your husband belongs to a group that is outside the fold of Islam, or if your husband decides to leave Islam, or if your husband does an act of riddah, something of this nature, that is a separate issue. And that is when we need to think about remaining or not remaining, because obviously it is not allowed for a Muslimah to be married to a non-Muslim.

This group is within the fold of Islam. And generally speaking, most of the groups that you are aware of, even if they have deviations, are within the fold of Islam. As I said, when will you consider a group outside the fold of Islam? When they do something or believe in something that is explicitly and clearly contradicting the kalimah itself: to believe in another god besides Allah, to not worship Allah. There are some groups out there that just don't have any shariah, any halal, any haram. There is no shariah, there is no five salah, there is no fasting of Ramadan, there is no Hajj, there is no recitation of the Qur'an. Those groups, there is no Islam. And again, these are the minority groups. But by and large, the mainstream groups that we are familiar with, that pray five times a day, that do wudu, that fast Ramadan, even if they have deviations that we disagree with, they are within the fold of Islam. **And therefore the nikah is valid, and it is up to her whether she wishes to remain or not.** And generally speaking, now that she has children, my sympathies would be for the family to remain together. And Allah knows best.
